listenings.text: Good morning, everyone. Ray Collins. Two minutes about last week, and then we start. It rained for five days and we lost three of them. I know. On Tuesday the water came down the ramp, one truck got stuck at the entrance, and six of you took shovels and spent the whole morning on it. On Wednesday I made the decision to close the lower area, and some of you were not happy with me. At eleven o'clock that area was under water. I am not saying I was right. I am saying we had nobody down there. Thursday and Friday we covered the machines, we went through the old reports, and we made a new schedule. And here is the good news from the office: the delay is three days, not seven. Nothing is broken. Now, this week.

Hi Giovanna, it is Karen. I saw your message about the rain and I laughed, sorry. Last March we had exactly the same week here in London. It started on a Monday, and by Wednesday there was a small flood in the lower tunnel. My supervisor said one thing only: everybody out. So we went up, we made tea, and we waited. I took photographs of the water for the report, and honestly they are the best photographs I have. Two things I learned that week. First, a storm is never a surprise here, so we always cover the machines on Friday afternoon, every Friday, even in July. Second, the delay was six days and nobody lost their job. Send me a photo of your mud. Talk soon.

extra_audio.text: On Monday the rain started at five in the morning. On Tuesday a truck got stuck in the mud at the entrance. On Wednesday Ray made the decision and closed the lower area. On Thursday the crew took plastic sheets and covered the machines. On Saturday the sun came back and the news was good.

paras: On Monday the rain started at five in the morning, and it did not stop for five days. Nobody on the site saw the sun again until Saturday. This is the story of that week, and of what the crew did with it.

On Tuesday the water came down the ramp and into the lower area. By nine o'clock there was mud everywhere, and one of the trucks got stuck at the entrance. Six people took shovels and worked on it for two hours. The truck came out, but the morning was gone.

On Wednesday Ray made a decision. He said one sentence to the crew: "Nobody goes underground today." Some people were not happy, because a delay costs money. Then, at eleven o'clock, there was a small flood in the lower area, exactly where the crew usually works. After that, nobody said anything about the decision.

On Thursday and Friday the crew did the work that rain cannot stop. They took plastic sheets and covered the machines and the new concrete. They went through the old reports, they made a new schedule, and they had two long meetings in the container. Karen called from London and said the same thing happens there every March.

On Saturday morning the sun came back, and the site got good news: the delay was three days, not seven. Everything was wet, but nothing was broken. A storm never asks permission. The only question is what you do with the days it takes from you.
